title: The real cost of your car: building a loan calculator with Next.js
label: Tutorial
description: Build and test a car loan calculator with Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind. Understand amortization, compare terms, and separate loan payments from purchase cost.
body:
A $35,000 car can become a $44,277.10 purchase without changing the car. In the example I used to build this tool, the difference comes from financing $30,000 at 8% APR for seven years, plus a $5,000 down payment. The monthly number looks much smaller than the full commitment.

I built **The Real Cost of Your Car** with Codex, Next.js, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS to make that relationship visible. You can change the price, down payment, APR, term, sales tax and fees, then inspect every monthly payment. This article explains the calculation and how to build the same kind of tool, including the decisions that make its results checkable.

[Open the car loan calculator](https://carcost.lautarogartner.com)

## A $35,000 car, three ways to pay

Start with the preset: a **$35,000 car**, **$5,000 down**, **8% APR**, and **no taxes or fees**. That leaves $30,000 to finance. Keep those inputs fixed and change only the term:

- **36 months:** $940.09 regular monthly payment, $3,843.28 total interest, $38,843.28 total purchase cost.
- **60 months:** $608.29 regular monthly payment, $6,497.52 total interest, $41,497.52 total purchase cost.
- **84 months:** $467.59 regular monthly payment, $9,277.10 total interest, $44,277.10 total purchase cost.

The seven-year payment is $472.50 lower than the three-year payment. In this fixed-rate example, it also adds **$5,433.82 in interest**. The comparison is useful because it holds the price and APR constant. These are mathematical scenarios, not offers from lenders or a claim about which term someone should choose.

The calculator compares 36, 48, 60, 72 and 84 months side by side. Selecting a column updates the main result, chart and schedule. A custom field also accepts whole-number terms from 1 to 120 months.

## Define the totals before writing the interface

The most consequential product decision was how to label the money. “Total paid” can mean different things, so the interface names each total explicitly:

- **Amount financed:** car price + sales tax + fees − down payment.
- **Total loan payments:** the sum of the monthly payments, including principal and interest. It excludes the down payment.
- **Total purchase cost:** total loan payments + down payment. It includes the taxes and fees entered into this calculator because those costs are financed.

For the 60-month preset, those amounts are $30,000.00 financed, $36,497.52 in loan payments, and $41,497.52 in purchase cost. Adding the down payment twice would overstate the result; leaving it out would understate the purchase cost.

The tax convention is deliberately visible: sales tax applies to the full car price, and all entered taxes and fees are financed. Local rules, trade-in credits and a lender's treatment of fees can differ. The tool does not try to infer a jurisdiction from a visitor's location.

Despite the name, this is a **purchase and financing calculator**, not a full ownership-cost model. Insurance, maintenance, depreciation, fuel and other ownership costs are excluded. That limit appears in the interface because a precise-looking number needs an equally precise definition.

## How the loan math works

The calculation uses standard fixed-rate monthly amortization. Let P be the amount financed, r the monthly rate, and n the number of payments. The regular payment is P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r) raised to −n). Here, r = APR ÷ 100 ÷ 12. At 0% APR, divide P by n instead.

This model treats the entered APR as a fixed nominal annual interest rate. A real lender's disclosed APR may include charges, and daily-interest contracts or different payment timing can produce different results. The tool is explicit about its simpler monthly assumptions.

Here is the small TypeScript core for the regular payment. The full source also validates the complete purchase inputs and builds the schedule:

```ts
function monthlyPayment(principal: number, apr: number, months: number) {
  if (![principal, apr, months].every(Number.isFinite) || principal < 0 || apr < 0 || !Number.isInteger(months) || months < 1) throw new RangeError("Invalid loan");
  const principalCents = Math.round(principal * 100);
  const rate = apr / 1200;
  const exactCents = rate === 0
    ? principalCents / months
    : principalCents * rate / -Math.expm1(-months * Math.log1p(rate));
  return principalCents === 0 ? 0 : Math.max(1, Math.round(exactCents)) / 100;
}
```

Math.log1p and Math.expm1 avoid subtracting nearly equal floating-point numbers when the rate is very close to zero. The special 0% branch makes the no-interest case readable. Keeping this calculation outside React also makes it straightforward to test without rendering the page.

For a $30,000 principal at 8% APR, the first month's interest is $200.00. With a $608.29 regular payment, $408.29 reduces the principal and the balance becomes $29,591.71. Next month, interest is calculated on that smaller balance.

## Make every monthly row reconcile

A correct annuity formula is only the start. A schedule also needs a consistent rounding rule. The implementation keeps the ledger in integer cents: round each month's interest, subtract it from the payment to get principal, and subtract that principal from the remaining balance.

The final payment clears the remaining balance rather than blindly repeating the regular amount. In the 60-month preset, the regular payment is $608.29 and the final payment is **$608.41**. The schedule therefore totals **$6,497.52** in interest. An unrounded theoretical calculation gives about $6,497.51; that one-cent difference comes from rounding monthly interest, not from a different loan formula.

Useful invariants are more convincing than a screenshot of the final result:

- For every row, payment = principal + interest.
- Each balance equals the previous balance minus that month's principal.
- The sum of principal paid equals the amount financed.
- The sum of all payments equals the displayed total loan payments.
- The final balance is zero and no displayed balance is negative.

With extremely small amounts, cent rounding can clear a loan before the requested term. A fully paid purchase has no repayment schedule. Those cases deserve deliberate states instead of a chart that silently divides by zero.

## Build the tool in small pieces

The app uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. Its calculation is local and deterministic; there is no application backend, account creation or quote API. The initial example renders as real page content, and editing the form updates browser state.

The project is split by responsibility:

```txt
src/lib/loan.ts                 calculation, validation and CSV
src/lib/loan.test.ts            amortization tests
src/components/loan-form.tsx    editable inputs and errors
src/components/cost-summary.tsx named financial totals
src/components/payment-chart.tsx principal/interest exploration
src/components/loan-comparison.tsx five shared-rate scenarios
src/components/payment-schedule.tsx monthly rows and export
src/components/calculator.tsx   state and composition
```

First, build the pure calculation and validate it. Next, connect the form and the cost summary. Only then add comparisons and the chart, using the same calculation for every term. Finally, add schedule pagination and CSV export. That order keeps an attractive interface from getting ahead of the evidence behind its numbers.

For input state, keep what the visitor is typing separate from the last valid loan. Clearing an input or entering a down payment larger than the whole purchase shows an inline error and an explicit “last valid estimate” notice. It does not quietly clamp the value or present an old result as if it described the invalid input.

The chart is native SVG, so it does not need a large charting dependency. Pointer movement explores the monthly bars; a labeled range input provides keyboard and touch access to the same principal and interest amounts. The monthly table remains the exact numerical representation, and the CSV includes every payment rather than just the visible page.

The visual direction is black, graphite and silver, with system typography and restrained blue links. Wide comparison tables scroll inside their own region on a phone. Input labels, focus styles, semantic tables and reduced-motion support are part of making the tool usable, alongside its appearance.

## Run the exact example locally

[Download the tested source ZIP](/downloads/car-loan-calculator-source.zip)

Use Node.js 24 LTS. Unzip the download, open a terminal in its parent folder, then run:

```sh
cd car-loan-calculator
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:3000. The source includes its dependency lockfile so npm ci installs the recorded versions. Stop the development server before using the production preview on the same port.

```sh
npm test
npm run build
npm start
```

The 27 unit tests cover the preset, zero interest, one-month repayment, taxes and fees, cash purchases, invalid values, near-zero rates, CSV output and payment-by-payment reconciliation across all five comparison terms. The production build also validates TypeScript. Browser checks cover interaction and layout; passing unit tests alone would not establish that the page is usable on a phone or by keyboard.

If you adapt the code, start by changing one assumption and giving it a test. Extra payments, daily interest, trade-in tax credits and separately paid fees each change the model. They should not be added as cosmetic switches that leave the existing formula untouched.

## Publish a static tool, keep the assumptions visible

The Next.js configuration uses a static export:

```ts
const config = { output: "export" };
export default config;
```

After the build, the deployable files are in the out directory. This calculator is hosted on Vercel at its own subdomain, while the article lives on my main website. Vercel supplies the project's CNAME target and HTTPS certificate; the DNS record is configured at the domain's authoritative DNS provider. Use the target supplied for your own project rather than copying a DNS value from a tutorial.

The deployment serves the exported HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Visitors can use the calculator without submitting their numbers to an application API. I also keep the result definitions, rounding rule and exclusions beside the experience, so readers can understand what the tool actually estimates.

## Try it, inspect it, change one thing

Open the preset, compare 36 and 84 months, then move through the chart. Look at the total interest and purchase cost alongside the monthly payment. Next, try 0% APR or a down payment covering the full price and see whether the result behaves as expected.

That is what I wanted from this project: a small tool whose math, interface and limits can be checked. Codex helped build it; the useful part is being able to inspect the result instead of trusting the polish.

[Try The Real Cost of Your Car](https://carcost.lautarogartner.com)

[See the project and screenshots](/work/carcost)

## Sources and illustration downloads

The financial context follows the [CFPB guide to comparing auto loans](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-compare-auto-loan-offers-what-should-i-look-at-besides-the-monthly-payment-en-753/). The implementation references [Next.js static exports](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/static-exports) and [Vitest's testing guide](https://vitest.dev/guide/). All quoted amounts above come from this tool's stated illustrative inputs, not from lender pricing.

The original AI-generated concept illustrations are visual metaphors, not data charts or screenshots. Download the full-resolution files: [car and payment road, 4K](/articles/car-loan/cover-4k.jpg), [principal and interest, 4K](/articles/car-loan/amortization-4k.jpg), and [interface, calculation and tests, 4K](/articles/car-loan/build-4k.jpg). The page uses smaller optimized versions. The 4K downloads are upscaled exports of the generated originals, not native 4K renders.
